banner.title: THE DSG PLOT AND COUNTERPLOT, R552: printed pp. 103-106 (pdf 104-107) - the storytelling doctrine: the chapter head (the story just as important as the world setting, perhaps the most important campaign element; the DM as bard or storyteller creating heroic fantasy with a few imaginative players, many DMs leaving room for improvement); The Story Structure (unchanged since writing developed, the ancient hearth storytellers exploiting it; the exposition introducing location and circumstances with main-conflict hints, arousing curiosity and motivating participation; the development with its gradual plot learning and rising tension, long stories carrying several climaxes; the climax resolving the major conflicts, the showdown with the evil source, satisfactory only after lesser challenges lead closer; the denouement as short retrospection - victors spoils, vanquished losses, PCs asking questions, basking in glory; all elements present with the timing to the storyteller); Exposition (the long-NPC-speech mistake boring the players into a bad start; the acted-out encounter with questions; the maps, characters and documents handouts; involvement beating passive reception; the information cards read aloud with the format fit - the parliament speaker roles - kept as references; the immediate combat opener especially for Adventurer-types, forcing teamwork, the attackers revealing vague clues during the attack or through prisoner confessions; combat before the speech, players more willing to listen; the between-session advance information a few days ahead for ahead-of-time plans); Development (occupying more game time than all other elements combined, ideally multiple techniques; the minion encounters teaching the opposition - creature types, enthusiasm, training and equipment, motivation to serve the master; the noncombat prods - sages, seers, beggars, puzzling notes, cipher-concealed maps; not all development encounters advancing the plot, the random encounters as sudden challenge and combat, feedback deciding when combat is needed; combat eventually pointing to the climax, a semi-climactic encounter for the final combat of the evening making each session a short story); Climax (careful planning with game balance the primary requirement, no fiddling, the intelligently-run PCs holding a reasonable chance with escape possibilities on failure; more than a straight melee - mental with the physical, facing the adversary who controlled the evil forces, typically in its lair but not necessarily; the possibility of claiming character lives even in victory, no character needing to perish but sufficient challenge requiring deadly potential; the adversary tactics tailored to leader intelligence, the fight as important to them, the special aid against well-equipped PCs, the emergency escape route - neither villains nor heroes necessarily dying, the always-escaping-villain campaigns; several potential solutions, creative responses allowed, more than one route to success; the staging with dramatic visual effects, perilous terrain, portentous occasion - the evil temple or the fiery-chasm bridge against the random corridor; make it dramatic - threatened and exhilarated, tense with the outcome in doubt to the end, failure still significant unless through poor play or lack of cooperation, the key goal that everybody has fun); Denouement (tying up loose ends; perusing the foe's area, the choice magic item or two, the clues answering questions, the rescued grateful prisoners; the time of safety, the minor encounter anticlimactic, the arrogant PCs surprised as a reminder, nothing cast in stone; the next-adventure lead, the related adversary, avoiding the inn-and-mysterious- stranger opening); Multiple Story Lines (more than one story at a time, tailored to the player types, the long-running framework with per-session stories, lines dropped and resumed; the sequential series sharing a grand purpose - the heroic epic, a single story with many episodes, the fine noble broad purpose: saving a world or nation, defending a god or religion, exploring a vast uncharted realm; the good-aligned main characters and the good-sanctioned cause, the participants changed usually for the better, the purpose gained at some cost; the years-spanning conflict, the isolated challenges as sessions, the level advancement, the small victories as rewards beyond gold and magic; the momentum demand - the session-ending plot climax, the major objective every 3-4 sessions; the cliffhanger with its remarkably low player tolerance, used rarely and only after a successful session climax; the periodic changes - the new epic every year or so, the occasional unrelated side encounter with a meaningful reward, the periodic clues that the epic goal grows closer); and the Story Elements head with The Villains (the antagonist as any blocking force including weather, most often a living being, possibly several; the unintelligent foes worthy of single-session stories, the minimal-intelligence foes more rewarding with more tactical options and epic length; the villain hierarchy with its minor antagonists and the chief's identity as an early objective, all levels attended; the unique villain NPCs beyond the biggest orc; the familiarization without confrontation - hirelings naming him, the discovered messages, the victims' tales; the personal confrontation relished as culmination; the bumbling buffoon as the low-ranking exception; the main antagonist equal to the party together or protected by bodyguards, traps, fortifications, disguises; the surviving villain - the last-minute escape, the return promise, the rising-from-the-dead, the future structure and built-in motivation, the returning villain's power increased to maintain game balance) and the Foreshadowing opener (the vague hints, portents, dreams and clues that something is going to happen; the suspense and mystery; the warning use with the deadly trap foreshadowed - the black-hole message scrawled in blood, the exact nature unrevealed, the PCs on guard; the Problem-Solver affinity, the variety discipline, the augury invitation - the section crossing the pp. 106-107 boundary and completing next round).

bools.comment: the story designed for the players is just as important as the world setting; the story line may be the most important element in the campaign
bools.name: dceStoryEqualWorld

bools.comment: the DM's function may be viewed as a bard or storyteller creating heroic fantasy with a few imaginative players; many DMs leave room for improvement, and the suggestions improve the skill and the fun
bools.name: dceDMAsBard

bools.comment: standard story structure has changed little since writing developed; the ancient hearth storytellers understood and exploited it; the wise DM uses the time-honored technique
bools.name: dceStructureAncient

bools.comment: the exposition introduces location and circumstances, often hints the story's main conflict, arouses the players' curiosity and motivates them to take part
bools.name: dceExpositionDefines

bools.comment: development lets the players gradually learn the plot with rising tension as the stakes or danger become clear; a long story should have several climaxes along the way
bools.name: dceDevelopmentTension

bools.comment: the climax resolves one or more major conflicts - the showdown between the PCs and the evil source they faced; satisfactory only after the characters overcame lesser challenges leading closer
bools.name: dceClimaxDefines

bools.comment: the denouement is a short retrospection: victors enjoy spoils and review accomplishments, the vanquished count losses; the PCs ask questions, basking in glory before the next challenge
bools.name: dceDenouementDefines

bools.comment: all the structural elements should be present in a DM's story; the exact timing and placement is left to the storyteller's judgment
bools.name: dceAllElementsPresent

bools.comment: the common mistake: a long detailed NPC speech the PCs must sit through and obey - players almost always find it boring and the DM is off to a bad start
bools.name: dceSpeechMistake

bools.comment: instead of reading an introduction, act out an encounter with an important NPC, giving players the opportunity to ask questions
bools.name: dceActOutEncounter

bools.comment: distribute maps, characters, documents, or other handouts to the players
bools.name: dceHandouts

bools.comment: PCs involved in the exposition enjoy it much more than passively receiving the same information
bools.name: dceInvolvementBeatsPassive

bools.comment: the information cards read aloud at the game's start, the players introducing each other to the story; the format fit - each player assuming a speaker's role at a parliament or town council; the cards kept as handy references
bools.name: dceInformationCards

bools.comment: engage the PCs in a combat encounter immediately - especially effective with Adventurer-types; it forces teamwork and immediate involvement; the attackers reveal vague clues during the attack or through prisoner confessions
bools.name: dceCombatOpener

bools.comment: after a combat encounter the DM can spend more time on exposition; precede the long speech with combat - players more willing to listen
bools.name: dceCombatBeforeSpeech

bools.comment: when players and DM can communicate between sessions, provide expository information a few days ahead; the players make plans ahead of time
bools.name: dceAdvanceInformation

bools.comment: development occupies more game time than all other structural elements put together; ideally the DM employs more than one technique
bools.name: dceDevelopmentLongest

bools.comment: encounters bearing a relationship to the primary villain develop the story - battling the foe's minions teaches the opposition: creature types, enthusiasm, training and equipment, motivation to serve the master
bools.name: dceMinionsTeach

bools.comment: sages, seers, beggars and other NPCs serve as gentle prods toward the right direction; puzzling notes and cipher-concealed maps provide clues
bools.name: dceNoncombatProds

bools.comment: not all developmental encounters need advance the plot; random encounters create sudden challenge and combat; feedback decides when a combat encounter is necessary
bools.name: dceRandomBalance

bools.comment: combat eventually points the characters toward the climax; arrange a semi-climactic encounter for the final combat of the evening, making each gaming session a short story in its own right
bools.name: dceSemimax

bools.comment: the climactic encounter carefully planned with game balance the primary requirement - no fiddling necessary; balanced so intelligently-run PCs have a reasonable chance of overcoming, with possibilities for escape if they fail
bools.name: dceBalancePrimary

bools.comment: the climax should involve more than a straight sword-swinging spell-casting melee - mental as well as physical challenges, facing the adversary who controlled the evil forces, typically in its lair but not necessarily
bools.name: dceMentalPhysical

bools.comment: a climactic encounter should include the possibility of claiming one or more characters' lives even if the party wins; no character need perish, but sufficient challenge requires a foe with deadly potential
bools.name: dceDeadlyPotential

bools.comment: tailor the adversary tactics to the leaders' intelligence; the fight as important to them as to the PCs; allow special aid against well-equipped PCs; the emergency escape route - neither villains nor heroes must necessarily die
bools.name: dceAdversaryTactics

bools.comment: some of the most enjoyable long-running campaigns center on PCs trying to finish off a powerful villain who always seems to escape at the last minute
bools.name: dceEscapingVillain

bools.comment: the climactic encounter should allow several potential solutions; be flexible with creative responses; a given encounter should have more than one route to success
bools.name: dceMultipleSolutions

bools.comment: consider the staging - dramatic visual effects, perilous terrain, portentous occasion; the evil temple or the bridge swaying over a fiery chasm beats a randomly generated corridor
bools.name: dceStagingDrama

bools.comment: make it dramatic: the PCs threatened and exhilarated, the outcome in doubt to the very end; even failure significant unless through poor play or lack of cooperation; the setting adds to the drama; the key goal is that everybody has fun
bools.name: dceDramatic

bools.comment: the denouement ties up loose ends: perusing the foe's area, perhaps a choice magical item or two, clues answering questions, the newly rescued grateful prisoners as sources
bools.name: dceLooseEnds

bools.comment: a time of safety - the major foe overthrown, a minor encounter anticlimactic; not cast in stone: overly arrogant PCs can receive a sudden surprise attack as a reminder of their limitations
bools.name: dceSafety

bools.comment: the denouement often provides information leading to the next adventure - the related adversary keeping the plot moving, avoiding the same old gathered-at-the-inn mysterious-stranger opening
bools.name: dceNextAdventure

bools.comment: a good campaign usually relies on more than one story at a time, tailored to the player types; a long-running story frameworks the campaign while each session tells a story within itself; lines dropped and resumed
bools.name: dceMultipleLines

bools.comment: sequential stories sharing one grand purpose emulate the heroic epic: a single story with many episodes, each interrelated adventure bringing the fine noble purpose closer - broad scope like saving a world or nation, defending a god or religion, exploring a vast uncharted realm
bools.name: dceEpicForm

bools.comment: epic main characters are traditionally good-aligned; the grand purpose good-sanctioned; participants often changed for the better; the purpose, if achieved, gained at some cost to the heroes
bools.name: dceEpicGood

bools.comment: an epic provides an overriding conflict lasting years of play; the isolated challenges make ideal one-or-several-session adventures; PCs advance in level; the small victories become rewards beyond gold and magical items
bools.name: dceEpicYears

bools.comment: an epic must move along or the goal seems unattainable; the objectives challenging and dramatic; each session ideally ends with some sort of plot climax
bools.name: dceEpicMomentum

bools.comment: the cliffhanger alternative places the PCs in an unresolved predicament; players have remarkably low tolerance, so use it rarely and only after a successful session climax
bools.name: dceCliffhangerRare

bools.comment: keep the game exciting: a new epic every year or so; the occasional side encounter unrelated to the epic but carrying a meaningful reward; periodic clues showing the epic goal gradually growing closer
bools.name: dcePeriodicChanges

bools.comment: the antagonist is any force blocking the PCs' goals - weather or natural phenomena included - most often a living being, possibly represented by more than one creature
bools.name: dceAntagonistAnyForce

bools.comment: unintelligent foes - a marauding band of cave bears - make worthy opponents for short, single-session stories
bools.name: dceUnintelligentFoes

bools.comment: a foe of at least minimal intelligence is more interesting and rewarding, presenting many more tactical options and supporting stories of considerable, even epic, length
bools.name: dceMinimalIntelligence

bools.comment: long stories and epics need a villain hierarchy: early adventures against minor antagonists, learning the chief bad guy's identity a rewarding early objective; attend to all levels, not just the top
bools.name: dceVillainHierarchy

bools.comment: make villains unique NPCs - the orc chieftain developed beyond 'the biggest orc in the dungeon', with unique appearance and personality characteristics
bools.name: dceUniqueVillains

bools.comment: familiarize the PCs with the villain without confrontation: hirelings naming him in combat or captivity, discovered messages revealing his nature, victims' tales of terror and woe
bools.name: dceFamiliarization

bools.comment: familiarization adds the personal touch making the final confrontation very exciting - an individual sought over time and relished as culmination, not miscellaneous monsters
bools.name: dcePersonalConfrontation

bools.comment: not all villains need be menacing foci of evil power - a bumbling buffoon can occasionally serve as an effective low-ranking villain
bools.name: dceBuffoon

bools.comment: the main antagonist should be equal in power to the party of PCs taken together, or protected by an extensive series of bodyguards, traps, fortifications, or disguises; vanquishing him a challenging and dangerous encounter
bools.name: dceMainVillainPower

bools.comment: the villain need not be slain to be vanquished: the last-minute escape leaving henchmen and holdings in shambles with a promise to return, or even returning from the dead; a ready-made future structure and built-in motivation; the returning villain's power increased to maintain the established game balance
bools.name: dceVillainSurvives

bools.comment: foreshadowing means vague hints, portents, dreams, or other clues that something is going to happen; it builds suspense and increases mystery while familiarizing players with the obstacles in their path
bools.name: dceForeshadowDefines

bools.comment: foreshadowing as warning: a very deadly trap's existence and some means of recognizing it foreshadowed - the 'Beware the chamber of the black hole' message scrawled in blood, the exact nature unrevealed, the PCs on guard
bools.name: dceForeshadowWarning

bools.comment: foreshadowing is particularly effective for Problem-Solver players - many opportunities for challenging puzzles and riddles; vary the type (corridor after corridor of bloody writing loses its impact); players themselves invite it - an augury spell is an invitation to foreshadow
bools.name: dceForeshadowPuzzlers

consts.comment: a major objective accomplished every 3-4 sessions, the minimum
consts.name: dceObjectiveSessionsMin

consts.comment: a major objective accomplished every 3-4 sessions, the maximum
consts.name: dceObjectiveSessionsMax

consts.comment: keep the game exciting with periodic changes: create a new epic every year or so
consts.name: dceEpicRefreshYears

examples.note: the epic cadence: a major objective accomplished every 3-4 sessions.
the periodic changes: a new epic every year or so.
the structure: exposition, climax, denouement defined.
the exposition craft: the speech mistake, the combat opener, the cards.
the climax doctrine: balance, deadly potential, multiple solutions.
the surviving villain: the escape route and the returning foe.
the epic: the form, the rare cliffhanger.
the story elements: the villain hierarchy, the warning foreshadow.
